d.title: Every metric is a sentence that starts 'of all the'
d.caption: One confusion matrix on 297 held-out customers: TP 39, FN 9, FP 89, TN 160, prevalence 0.162. Each metric below reads a different slice of it — which is why 'what is the accuracy' is not a question the matrix can answer. The retention team means recall; the fraud team means precision; compliance means specificity.

d.title: Two constant predictors, and the metrics that see through them
d.caption: At 16.2% prevalence, predicting 'stay' for everyone scores **0.838 accuracy** — seventeen points above the actual model — while learning nothing at all. The metrics that cannot be fooled are the ones that collapse to 0 or 0.5 for a constant: AUC, F1, MCC. That is the test to apply to any metric before trusting it on an imbalanced problem.

d.title: Three averages over three classes
d.caption: The averaging choice decides whose errors count. Micro weights every **row** equally, so a small class failing badly disappears into it; macro weights every **class** equally, so the rare class's noisy metric gets a full third of the score. Neither replaces the per-class table.

cells.text: that the rare class is noisy

cells: the same as micro, slightly less

d.title: The ROC curve, one threshold at a time
d.caption: Ten scored rows, five positive. Walk the threshold down the sorted scores and watch the path: a **positive** steps the curve up, a **negative** steps it right. That is all an ROC curve is — the staircase of those steps. The area by trapezoids is 0.72, which equals 18/25: the number of positive–negative pairs the model ranked correctly, out of all 5 × 5 pairs.

d.title: ROC and PR answer different questions about the same ranking
d.caption: Both axes of ROC are within-class rates, so prevalence cannot move them — which makes ROC-AUC comparable across differently balanced datasets and blind to how rare the positives are. Precision mixes the classes, so PR tracks what acting on the flags will actually feel like.

d.title: What each metric is a function of
d.caption: The first row needs a threshold and the rest do not, which is the division that matters when selecting a model: choosing on accuracy or F1 means choosing a model **and** a threshold at once, and the threshold is usually the default 0.5 nobody examined.

d.title: One fitted model, eleven thresholds, three different answers
d.caption: Nothing changes down this table except the cut. Watch the three rules disagree: **cost** is minimised at 0.15, **F1** peaks at 0.25, and the default 0.50 is near-worst on both while flagging only 13 of 297 customers. The default is not a neutral choice, it is an unexamined one — and the sweep costs one line of code.

d.title: Four rules, four thresholds, from the same curve
d.caption: The sweep produces one table; which row you take is a business decision with four common shapes. Only the third uses the probability as a number, which is why it is the only one that needs the model to be calibrated (2.5).

nodes.label: The sweep
nodes.sub: precision, recall, cost at every cut

nodes.label: Fixed capacity
nodes.sub: top k by score; recall is the outcome

d.title: The decision picks the metric, and the metric picks the threshold
d.caption: Each row is a different thing going wrong when you are wrong, and therefore a different rule. The last one is the case people model incorrectly most often: when capacity is fixed, neither precision nor recall is the objective — the top k is, and recall is the outcome you report.
cells: take k by score; report recall

d.title: Five errors of 10, 10, 5, 12, 10 — under every regression metric
d.caption: One set of five errors, nine metrics. The **RMSE/MAE ratio of 1.03** is the diagnostic worth knowing: near 1 means the errors are all about the same size, and a ratio of 2 or more means a few large misses dominate the squared metric. R² is 0.981 here only because predicting the mean would have been catastrophic (SS_tot 25,000), which is why R² flatters a model on a high-variance target.

state: each error over its own target

d.title: One outlier arrives, and the metrics part company
d.caption: The same five errors, plus one miss of 100. MAE multiplies by 2.61 because the outlier is divided by n; RMSE multiplies by **4.31**, because the square arrives before the average — 100² is 10,000 against 469 for the other five squares combined. The median does not move at all. And one row took forty points off R². Whenever RMSE and MAE diverge, a few rows own the squared metric, and those rows are worth reading individually.

d.title: Why MAPE cannot be used where it is asked for most
d.caption: MAPE divides by the actual, so a true value near zero produces an unbounded term, and one such row dominates the average. It is also asymmetric: under-forecasting is capped at 100% error while over-forecasting is not, so minimising MAPE systematically biases a forecast low.
cells: the bias is built in; use MAE

d.title: Which regression metric, decided by one question each
d.caption: The questions are about the **decision**, not the data. The loss a model trains on and the metric a business reads need not match — train on squared error because it is smooth, report MAE because operations understand it. What must match is the metric and the cost of being wrong.

cells.text: WAPE, or MAPE if no zeros

d.title: The random forest's reliability table: predicted against observed
d.caption: Bin the predictions into tenths and compare the mean prediction in each bin with the **observed** positive rate. A calibrated model's two columns match. The forest's do not: it says 0.046 where the truth is 0.026, and 0.656 where the truth is 0.959 — under-confident at both ends, because averaging 0/1 votes pulls every prediction toward the middle and cannot reach the extremes unless every tree agrees.

d.title: Each family is miscalibrated in its own characteristic direction
d.caption: The shape follows from the training objective. A forest averages 0/1 votes, which pulls every prediction toward the middle. Cross-entropy on a deep network pushes logits apart without bound, which is over-confidence by construction. Note the measured tension: the forest was the **best ranker** at 0.916 AUC and the **worst calibrated** at 0.070 ECE.

d.title: When calibration matters, and when it does not
d.caption: The dividing line is whether anything does **arithmetic** on the probability. Ranking and a validation-swept threshold use only the ordering, so a miscalibrated score is harmless there. A cost formula, an expected value, or a number shown to a person all treat p as a probability.

d.title: Three queries, graded 0 to 3, under every ranking metric
d.caption: q1 = [3,2,0,1,0], q2 = [0,0,3,0,1], q3 = [1,0,0,0,0]. Look at q3: a single weak result in the right place scores **NDCG 1.000**, because normalisation divides by the best possible ordering of what was available. And q2's perfect item sitting in slot 3 costs it half its NDCG. Position is the whole subject — the same set of results in a different order is a different prediction.

d.title: Scoring a clustering, with labels and without
d.caption: Internal indices measure the geometry a method produced, so they systematically prefer the kind of shape that method makes — on two moons, k-means scores a silhouette of 0.487 and the **true** labelling scores 0.328. External indices need labels and must be corrected for chance, which is why ARI and AMI exist and the raw Rand index does not belong in a report.
cells: prefers small k on a continuum

d.title: One model, four regions, four fairness criteria that disagree
d.caption: The same fitted model at the same threshold. Flag rate runs 0.30 to 0.39, TPR 0.62 to 0.73, FPR 0.22 to 0.33, and precision 0.23 to 0.44 — so a flag **means** nearly twice as much in east as in west. These criteria are mathematically incompatible when base rates differ, so the team must choose which one it is claiming, and say so.

d.title: The gain chart: cumulative share of churners captured, by decile
d.caption: Rank all 297 customers by score and cut into deciles. The **top decile holds a third of all churners** — a lift of 3.30 over calling at random — and calling half the base reaches 85% of them. This is the chart a retention team adopts without training, because 'the top 10% contains a third of the churners' is a sentence anyone can act on. Note the last two deciles add nothing: the model has already found everyone by decile 9.
d.label: decile 1 lift 3.30 · decile 5 lift 1.70 · decile 10 lift 1.00

d.title: Five fold scores, and what they do and do not support
d.caption: Mean 0.848, sd 0.044, standard error 0.020, naive interval 0.848 ± 0.055. That supports 'the procedure scores about 0.85, plausibly 0.79 to 0.90'. It does **not** support 'better than a model scoring 0.83' — 0.83 is inside the interval, and the folds' training sets overlap, so the five numbers are correlated and the true standard error is larger than 0.020.

d.title: Why the naive paired t-test over folds is wrong
d.caption: Cross-validation folds share training rows, so the per-fold differences are **not independent** — and a t-test that assumes they are reports an interval far too narrow and a p-value far too small. The corrections exist because the dependence is structural, not a sampling accident.
cells: when a stricter test is wanted
an interval on a single number

d.title: Two models, two intervals, and the only comparison that counts
d.caption: Logistic 0.789 and gbdt 0.772 look like a clear ordering until the intervals are drawn: they overlap almost entirely. The right object is the **paired** interval on the difference, computed on the same rows — 0.017 with a 95% interval of [−0.012, 0.049], which includes zero. 'Logistic is ahead' is the best guess; 'logistic is better' is not something 297 rows can support.

d.title: Offline is necessary and never sufficient
d.caption: Offline evaluation reads logged rows whose labels exist because some **past policy** chose to show them — so it answers 'which candidate looks most promising', not 'will this move the business'. Only the second question is the one the deployment is for, and only a randomised test answers it.
